subject: chemistry
question_text: Give an account of the properties of washing soda.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, IPE STUDY MATERIAL for Jr. Students — Chemistry (2026-27 edition), book p.88, chapter 7 s-BLOCK ELEMENTS, SAQ question 33. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints no per-step allocation on any answer in this chapter. This book prints no exam-appearance years for this chapter, so appearances[] is empty — the chapter has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. THE TWO DEHYDRATION TEMPERATURES ARE NCERT'S OWN FIGURES: about 375 K for the loss of nine water molecules and above 373 K for the last one. Every equation was checked atom by atom: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O → Na₂CO₃·H₂O + 9H₂O (H 20 = 20, O 13 = 13); Na₂CO₃·H₂O → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O; Na₂CO₃ + 2H₂O → 2Na⁺ + 2OH⁻ + H₂CO₃ (H 4 = 4, O 5 = 5, charge 0 = 0); CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ (charge −2 = −2); Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂ → CaCO₃ + 2NaCl and Na₂CO₃ + MgCl₂ → MgCO₃ + 2NaCl. TWO ADDITIONS BEYOND THE SOURCE ANSWER, both standard syllabus content and both to be confirmed by a teacher: the ionic hydrolysis form CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ is given alongside the book's molecular form because the NCERT text uses the ionic one and both are correct; and the two water-softening equations are carried because the softening action is the chemical property the substance is named for. HYDROLYSIS ARROW: the carbonate hydrolysis is an equilibrium, so both the molecular and the ionic form are printed with the equilibrium arrow. A full arrow would claim complete conversion to carbonic acid, which is not what happens; the source book prints a full arrow, and a student who writes one is not making an error.

steps.label: What washing soda is
lines: Washing soda is sodium carbonate
decahydrate, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
It is a white crystalline solid.
It is readily soluble in water.
Its solution in water is alkaline and
not neutral.
steps.why: An account of properties has to open with the substance itself: the formula fixes the ten water molecules that the heating equations then remove, and the ready solubility is what makes the alkaline solution possible at all.
common_mistakes: Writing the formula as Na₂CO₃. Washing soda is the decahydrate Na₂CO₃·10H₂O; the anhydrous salt is soda ash.
Confusing it with baking soda. Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO₃.
steps.memory_tip: Washing soda carries ten water molecules: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
steps.margin_note: Open with the formula; the later steps all rest on it.

steps.label: Action of heat
lines: On heating to about 375 K it loses nine
of its ten water molecules and gives the
monohydrate:
Above 373 K the last water molecule goes
and anhydrous soda ash is left:
steps.why: The water leaves in two stages and not in one, and the white powder called soda ash is only the end of the second stage — writing both equations with their temperatures is what shows that.
common_mistakes: Removing all ten water molecules in one step. Nine leave first and the monohydrate is formed.
Calling the product of the first stage soda ash. Soda ash is the anhydrous salt formed above 373 K.
steps.memory_tip: Nine water molecules first, then the tenth: decahydrate, monohydrate, soda ash.
steps.margin_note: Two equations and two temperatures belong in this step.

steps.label: The alkaline solution
lines: Washing soda is the salt of a strong
base and a weak acid, so it hydrolyses
in water and gives hydroxide ions:
The ionic form says the same thing:
The solution therefore turns red litmus
blue.
steps.why: The alkaline solution is the property behind every cleaning use of washing soda, and it arises because the carbonate ion takes a proton from water and leaves a hydroxide ion behind.
common_mistakes: Saying the solution is neutral because it is a salt. The salt of a strong base and a weak acid gives an alkaline solution.
Writing the sodium ion as the one that hydrolyses. It is the carbonate ion that takes a proton from water.
steps.memory_tip: Strong base with weak acid gives an alkaline solution.
steps.margin_note: Both forms of the equation are correct; write whichever one you learned.

steps.label: Action on hard water
lines: Its solution reacts with the soluble
calcium and magnesium salts of hard
water and changes them into insoluble
carbonates:
This is why it is used in laundry and in
the glass, soap and paper industries.
steps.why: This is the property the substance is named for: the hardness is removed because the calcium and magnesium ions leave the solution as solid carbonates, so soap is no longer used up on them.
common_mistakes: Saying it removes only temporary hardness. It removes permanent hardness too, because the carbonate removes the calcium and magnesium ions as solid carbonates.
Leaving out the precipitate. The carbonates formed are insoluble and settle out of the solution.
steps.memory_tip: The carbonate takes calcium and magnesium out of the water as solids.
steps.margin_note: Close with the softening action; it is the property behind the name.

insider_note: The account is complete when it carries all four parts: the formula with its ten water molecules, the two stages of heating, the alkaline solution, and the softening of hard water.
